title: St Valentine
hookLine: an early Christian martyr whose day became about love, 14 February

cards: Red paper hearts taped to a classroom window. A drugstore aisle that turns pink overnight. Roses by the bucket, and a wait for every table.
In plenty of countries, February the fourteenth has become the day for saying I love you out loud.

But the name on the day belongs to someone the cards never mention: a Christian remembered as a martyr, whose story is mostly lost. Today starts a short run of days of love, kept by different traditions.

teach.b: First, the honest part. Tradition says Valentine was a Christian in the early centuries of the church, in or near Rome, who was put to death for his faith. Beyond that, the record is thin.
Old church lists remember more than one martyr named Valentine, and it isn't clear whether the stories are about one man or several. When the sources are this quiet, it's worth saying so.

Second, the stories people tell. One legend has him marrying couples in secret when marriage was forbidden to soldiers. Another has him healing his jailer's daughter and leaving her a note signed, from your Valentine.
These are stories, told and retold, not facts anyone can check, and they're loved anyway. Third, how a martyr's day became a lovers' day.
Long afterward, the English poet Geoffrey Chaucer wrote a poem, the Parliament of Fowls, set on Saint Valentine's day, when every bird comes to choose its mate.
Some scholars think that poem, and others like it, helped tie the saint's day to romance. Nobody can say for certain how the change happened.

Fourth, what's left when the legends are set aside: a person remembered by Christians as faithful unto death, and a day the world uses to say, plainly, I love you. Some churches still remember him on that day.
And one modern custom fits the legend of the note: writing it down, telling someone on paper what they mean to you.

how: Some churches still keep a feast of St Valentine on February 14, and around the world the day is marked by giving cards, notes and flowers to partners, friends and family.

games.why: tradition remembers a Christian martyr in or near Rome. the secret weddings and the note are legends, loved but unproven.

practice: Bring to mind one person who would be glad to hear from you, a partner, a parent, a friend, a teacher, a child, not necessarily the obvious one, and let their face come clear.

Then let one true, plain sentence form about what they mean to you, something like you made that year easier, and hold it until it feels right. If you pray, you can give thanks for them in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: St Valentine. A Christian remembered as a martyr, little known for certain, whose day became a day for telling people you love them. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a note. One plain sentence can carry a lot of love. Until tomorrow.
